# Standing instructions

How I want an agent to work in any of my projects. A project's own file is
more specific than this one and wins wherever the two disagree.

## Architecture

- **Hexagonal.** The domain and its ports are the centre. Everything that
  talks to the outside world is an adapter around it. A dependency points
  inwards, never outwards.
- **The core stays technology-free.** No Spring, no Jackson, no JDBC, no
  HTTP client type in a core module. A framework is a detail of one adapter,
  and a detail must not leak into the thing it serves.
- **A port is named for what the domain needs**, not for what implements it.
  `MessageRepository`, not `PostgresMessages`. If the name only makes sense
  once you know the technology, it is in the wrong place.
- **One reason to change per class.** A class that both decides and persists
  is two classes that have not been separated yet.
- **Small interfaces.** A port with three methods that every implementation
  needs beats one with twelve where most throw `UnsupportedOperationException`.
- **Composition over inheritance.** Inherit only from something written to be
  inherited from.

## Extending

- A new capability is a **new implementation of an existing port**, not
  another branch inside existing code. When a change means adding a case to
  a `switch` or an `if` in the core, the shape is wrong: ask whether it wants
  a port.
- Prefer a seam that already exists over a new one. Two seams doing almost
  the same job is worse than one that is slightly less convenient.
- Configuration belongs at the edge, injected. Static mutable state is not
  configuration, it is a trap.

## Reuse

- **Look before you add.** Search the codebase for something that already
  does this. Reuse beats a second, nearly identical implementation, even when
  the second one is nicer.
- A module should be usable **on its own**, without adopting the whole stack.
  If using one part drags in three others, the seams are in the wrong places.
- Where a technology-independent solution is available at reasonable cost,
  take it. Where it is not, isolate the dependency behind a port and say so
  in a comment, so the next person knows it is a deliberate edge and not an
  oversight.
- Do not build for an imagined future. Build the seam the current change
  needs, cleanly, so the next change is cheap.

## Simplicity

- The simplest thing that is actually correct. Fewer concepts, fewer layers,
  fewer options.
- Delete rather than deprecate, while the project is young.
- If you have to explain a design at length for it to make sense, it is a
  sign to simplify, not to write more explanation.

## How to work

- **Read before you write.** Find the code, understand what it does, then
  change it.
- Small steps that can each be verified. Not one large change that stands or
  falls as a whole.
- **Run the build and the tests before you say something works**, and say
  what you ran. If you could not verify it, say that plainly instead of
  implying success.
- A test earns its place by failing when the behaviour breaks. Check that it
  does, by breaking the behaviour on purpose once.
- When something is blocked or you are unsure, say so early and say what you
  need. Do not guess quietly.

## Writing

- **German with me in the chat, English in everything that lands in a
  repository**: code, comments, javadoc, commit messages, pull requests,
  documentation.
- Comments explain *why*, not *what*. The code already says what.
- Name things for what they mean in the domain, not for their type or their
  pattern.
